terms.definition: A workshop technique (Alberto Brandolini) for modeling a business domain as a timeline of domain events, then filling in the commands, aggregates, policies, read models, actors, and external systems around them. This tool recovers a first-draft Event Storming model directly from code instead of a from-scratch workshop, so the result is an always-true scaffold and conversation starter rather than a replacement for the wall.

The shared domain vocabulary that the code, the model, and the people all use for the same concept. Drift (the same concept under two ids/names) is what the merge's consistency pass hunts. Phase 5 promotes the vocabulary into a first-class curated glossary (the terms this file authors), distinct from the behavioral stickies.

A consistency boundary: state that changes together and enforces its own invariants. In Event Storming an aggregate only RECEIVES commands and EMITS events, never issues a command. In a services-and-repositories codebase there are no explicit aggregates, so the data-layer scout recovers them as clusters of entities that change together (they are almost always 'inferred').

An intent to change state, named in the imperative ("PlaceOrder", "MergeTraces"). Commands come from actors, policies, or external systems, are handled by an aggregate, and produce an event. A command that must read other aggregates/read models before acting expresses that with a 'reads' edge (a command lookup).

A named business fact that already happened, stated in the past tense ("OrderPlaced", "ModelValidated"). It is the most stable Event Storming convention. "A row was inserted" is NOT an event; the discriminator against a raw measurement/telemetry data-point is whether it is a domain-significant fact. Prefer few meaningful events over one event per statement (a multi-table transactional write is one event).

Strictly reactive logic: "whenever <event> then <command>." It sits after an event and before the next command, orchestrating cross-aggregate reactions. This repo adds a 'synchronous' flag: a synchronous policy is inline synchronous code reacting to the first event (not a decoupled subscriber), which is how the UI-vs-service split rule models a second write with its own failure window.

A constraint enforced INSIDE an aggregate while it handles a command, before any event, that can reject the action ("a bundle item references a real item at most once", "aggregates never issue commands"). It is NOT event-triggered and does not issue a command, which is exactly what distinguishes it from a Policy. Invariants attach to their aggregate with an 'enforces' edge and never appear in a flow's steps lane.

What an actor reads in order to decide: a grid, view, projection, or downloaded file. It is the query side, distinct from the command/write side, and carries a demand-driven fields[] list describing what data it returns and where that data comes from.

A system outside the deploy boundary (SaaS, another service, a cloud API, a legacy system, the local filesystem/browser/editor as this tool models them). It can issue commands and raise or receive events. An in-process library is NOT an external system. An aggregate whose state actually lives inside one is marked with 'ownedBy'.

A person or role that issues commands and reads read models to decide (Viewer, Operator, a connected Claude session). Actor is the softest color convention on a wall (a small yellow), and in a flat digital diagram it needs a genuinely different hue from the aggregate to stay distinct.

The red sticky: friction, risk, disagreement, or a place where intent is unrecoverable from code, framed as THE QUESTION A HUMAN SHOULD ANSWER and anchored to the source. Hotspots are the payoff of a code-derived model and the one thing no code reading can produce; they are human judgment. They attach at flow level and live in a top-level hotspots array, not in nodes.

One card on the Event Storming wall: a single command, aggregate, event, policy, read model, actor, external system, or invariant. In this tool a sticky is realized as a node in flows.json (behavioral stickies are colored by the event-storming palette). Value Objects and Entities are NOT stickies; tactical structure is implied on the wall, not drawn.

terms.term: ES grammar rule (aggregates never issue commands)
terms.definition: The self-reinforcing loop Actor/Policy/External-System -> Command -> Aggregate -> Event -> Policy -> Command, with read models fed off events. The one hard constraint the merge enforces at load time is that an aggregate may only receive commands and emit events, never issue one: an edge from an aggregate with verb 'issues' is an error. The other shapes (policies issue commands, command lookups) are left to author discipline.

This repo's key modeling stance: the command/aggregate/event/policy grammar fits TRANSACTIONAL domains (intent that can be rejected), but a dataflow/ETL/pipeline stretch is a different plane that continuously transforms immutable records and cannot reject anything. Model the two planes joined at a named seam (an anti-corruption/translation step): everything on the dataflow side is plumbing kept in a command's tactical detail, and only domain-significant facts crossing the seam are promoted to events. In this self-model the merge and generate steps are ETL kept single-plane for exactly this reason.

anchors.symbol: Conventions: dataflow stages are not aggregates

terms.definition: The zoom level at which the same action is modeled. A generic 'cmd-attach-file' in a file-attachment pattern flow and a specialized 'cmd-attach-files-to-line' inline in an ordering flow are the same action at two altitudes. The merge deliberately does NOT force-merge legitimate altitude variations: collapsing them breaks the ability to walk each flow as a self-contained story. Shared aggregates and external systems, not collapsed commands, carry the connective tissue between flows.

The two registers the model moves between. STRATEGIC = what the system does, why, and how its flows connect (the recovered Event Storming view). TACTICAL = how it is actually implemented: the call chain, key methods, data touched, carried on every behavioral node as a 'tactical' block of explanation + source anchors. Every sticky keeps tactical anchors precisely so a reader can move between the two planes freely; a strategic node with no way back to code is a dead end.

A per-node flag: true when the concept was RECOVERED from code that never names it (the usual case for behavioral stickies in a services-and-repositories codebase), false only when the code literally names the concept. Physical data-model nodes (server/database/table/column) default to inferred:false, the inverse of the behavioral layer, because the SQL names them outright. At merge time an explicit inferred:false wins over an inferred:true seeding.

A strategic boundary within which the ubiquitous language is consistent; edges that cross it are the integration points (an anti-corruption layer or published language). A bounded context must be DECLARED with an explicit label, never inferred from namespace/folder layout, because code layout is an accident rather than a domain fact. A code-derived view cannot recover context grouping on its own, which is one of the things it structurally loses versus a workshop wall.
terms.openQuestion: This recovered self-model is small enough to be a single context and does not declare bounded-context boundaries; a human who knows the intended architecture should say whether the recovery/explorer/MCP surfaces are meant to be separate bounded contexts and, if so, label them.
